en: A cruel and grievous affliction
Against which all the heroes assembled.
Some souls were crazed and leaderless,
Wanderers with no one to pursue them,
Torn apart without a chief.
Those who always resisted,
Standing upon their honor,
Were slaughtered to the last.
That gnawing sorrow subsided.
“O Almighty, restore to me
My land he ravaged,” they prayed.
They held a feast without stint,
Spending all they possessed.
Baitailak, son of Bakai,
Thus began speaking to the people,
Softly beginning his weighty words.
The son whose name was renowned
Conceived an unfathomable plan
And held a feast beyond all measure.
When he said, “Hear these words of mine,”
The multitude blessed by Kyzýr
Thickened together like curdled yogurt.
“Baitailak’s wisdom
Is manifest and exemplary;
What he says is right,” they said.
When all their livestock and wealth
Were lavishly scattered,
And the finest words were spoken,
No pleasure was left unfulfilled.
Men grappled on horseback for the kök-börü,
Until their poles bent,
And heroic warriors jousted.
The victors threw down their rivals,
And mocked one another;
The fallen were left empty-handed,
While the victors claimed the prize.
It became an unimaginable spectacle,
An immense feast:
“The feast of hero Seytek,” they said,
“The design of Kuyaly and the people,” they said,
“For they saved our lives from torment.
It is the feast of our lion,” they said.
They bared the great camels’ teeth,
Let their lower lips droop,
Made their two humps tower,
And their necks arch like ducks,
Their shaggy manes trailing.
All the multitude
They made shout aloud with joy.
They slaughtered bright-red riding camels
And mares with fat a span thick.
They slaughtered equally from all four kinds,
And laid out wealth in equal measure.
They slaughtered livestock of all four kinds
And raised a mountain of meat like Ala-Too.
They meant to gather
Every person upon the earth.
They made the dew seem a swelling lake;
The people gathered and joined their strength,
Assembling the entire nation without exception.
The air steamed with meat and fat,
The people rejoiced and the land overflowed.
“It is dear Seytek’s feast,” they said,
“He whose back is like the lofty Ala-Too,
For he defeated Sarybai,” they said.
There on the banks of Talas,
At the feast of hero Seytek,
The Russians ate their fill and departed,
Saying, “If this Seytek lives,
The eighteen thousand worlds
Will marvel at him.”
The Chinese ate their fill and departed,
Saying, “If this Seytek lives,
Upon every crooked mortal
He will bring destruction.”
For nine days they had
The treasury doors thrown open.
To orphans, the poor, and widows,
To paupers who owned no livestock,
They scattered wealth lavishly.
His generosity was revealed;
To the hungry and destitute,
To the weak and impoverished,
Without valuing wealth by so much as a hair,
They measured it out with a whip,
And ordered it given to them.
They set the people’s hearts at ease
And made rich all who had lacked.
They had Kushkun and Durkun sing,
And thus delighted the people.
Their hearts surged with joy,
And many among the people reveled.
Each solitary soul became as a thousand,
And each presence shone like the Night of Power.
“Father Seytek, hero Seytek,
May he be the bulwark of the people,”
Many among the people blessed him.
“We escaped certain slaughter,
We were spared an open grave;
From the wretch who ruled in our fathers’ day,
We escaped his wrath,” they said.
The people’s hearts had been oppressed;
“Let the people proclaim his glory,” they said,
And the people’s hearts were stirred.
They appealed to Khan Seytek,
As though now destined to see wonders,
And pronounced their blessing,
As though he would allot each one an inheritance.
Spoken words cannot describe their dignity;
Among the people giving blessings
There were saints and every kind of soul.
Among those pronouncing blessings,
Some wore white turbans large as cauldrons,
And when they cried out, their voices rang like the call to prayer.
Seated, they were broad as hearths;
Their mouths seemed thick as forearms,
And their haunches broad as an embrace.
They were masters of royal encampments,
Khans of many different kinds.
Crying “Allah!” they raised their hands
And turned their faces toward the qibla.
Their inspired spirits surged;
Was he perhaps a saintly hero,
An interpreter of moon and stars,
A companion of the magnanimous lion,
Ready to render faithful service
And raise the fallen standard again?
He had been born into this world
As though he alone had come
To help lion Manas prevail,
And provide him wise counsel—
A herald upheld by the spirits,
A saint in whom all gifts converged.
The time came when he could no longer rise.
The old man had indeed been a hero.
Was any man ever so long-lived?
His ears had grown deaf and unhearing,
His eyes blind and unseeing.
Dear uncle Bakai
Had become level with the black earth,
His beard still full upon his chin.
That year, for Bakai,
The hour came to depart on his journey,
To leave this world without returning;
His time to go had come.
Alas, when the fatal guest, death,
Has come to pass,
When the eyes close and are sealed,
And its hour arrives,
When, alas, the head
Must enter the dark grave—
Here is the tale of your valiant father Bakai
At the hour of his death:
Raising their palms, wailing,
Lifting their hands, lamenting,
“Give your blessing before you die,” they said;
“Father Bakai, venerable elder,
Look upon your grandson,” they said.
When Bakai spread his palms:
“The people wept, every soul wept,
The whole vast nation wept,
All who wore turbans wept,
The learned mullahs wept,
Every white-bearded elder wept,
All the people, not one left out, wept.
All those who wept
Wept deeply from their sorrow,
For when every gray-maned hero,
Every mortal born,
Leaves descendants behind,
A man does not die,” they wept.
He was a soul grown exceedingly old;
Your gray-maned uncle Bakai
Had reached a great age.
Facing death,
He had grown too feeble even to crawl.
It was his destined hour;
Alas, your uncle Bakai
Had been overtaken by old age.
His raven-dark eyes were bloodshot,
His beard beneath his chin had whitened:
It was his hour to die!
No second one will come into the world;
Your forefather, old Bakai,
Will never return or be found again.
He was noble, he was a lion,
His fortune was complete;
The Creator will never again
Create a soul like Bakai.
The people wailed and the nation grieved,
They stood engulfed in clamor;
Unmatched among true men,
He stood amid the tumult.
If only the thoroughbred never tired,
If only frail man never aged,
If only the wide world never narrowed,
And each might live as he desired;
If only the mighty, boundless Creator
Would let all remain in its proper course,
I would have no regret—
If only it were so.
A man observes this and reflects,
Shaking his head and crying, “Alas!”
His body went slack as night descended,
And he turned his face toward death.
“Alas, he has fallen beyond recovery,” they said;
“This cruel, faithless, lying world!
Our mighty father Bakai
Has come to nothing,” they said.
“The teeth with which he ate his food
Have fallen out,” they said.
“The strength that kindled fire in both hands
Has left him,” they said.
“His feet that bore him
Down the slopes,
Alas, brave heart, have failed,” they said.
“The dreadful curse of affliction
Has wholly consumed him,” they said.
The season of courage and valor
Had passed away like this.
When old age came upon him,
The gray-maned hero Bakai
Had no flesh left, only bone,
Scarcely a spoonful of blood beneath his chin—
A creature reduced to crawling.
In your prime, splendid in sable,
You used to wear it proudly;
When black night fell upon the Kyrgyz,
You plunged into the clash.
Overcoming all who grappled with you,
How many peoples we used to rout!
His fortune was complete,
He was a lion upheld by the spirits;
While ancestral power and honor remain,
A man never truly dies.
He gathered the wealth of the world;
Across the whole universe
He sought ancestral lands—
Bakai was a lion among heroes.
Clad in blue lynx fur,
Bearing a blue-mottled shield,
He blinded those he marked
And ruled the whole world.
No enemy reached his frontier,
Nor did he live off the treasury.
Great was your dignity, fierce your wrath,
Alas, our forefather Bakai.
One day is light and one day night—
This accursed, fleeting world:
Behold how false it is,
How it parts one from one’s companion
And leaves one behind.
His beard had whitened like a swan;
When the day of his journey came,
Behold how he was parted
From Manas, his companion in time.
